other-interests-b2adc15591.headline: ‘Multifunctional’ brain implant translates speech and gestures in real time
other-interests-b2adc15591.fulltext:
Human communication relies on more than just talking; we nod, shrug, move our hands and point with our fingers. For people with severe paralysis, brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) can convey intended speech or movement. Now, researchers have shown that a single brain implant can do both at once.
The device, described1 today in Nature Neuroscience, is the first to translate both verbal and non-verbal modes of communication, simultaneously and within seconds of the user’s intent. It uses artificial intelligence to convert electrical brain activity into text that appears on screen and to prompt a personalized animated avatar to move.
Recent BCI technology has enabled people with paralysis to do tasks such as talking2 and controlling a cursor3 or a robotic arm4. “But most of these studies have focused on restoring one of these functions at a time,” says study co-author Samantha Brosler, a PhD student in bioengineering at the University of California, San Francisco.
This system is a proof of concept but aims to be “a step towards more multifunctional BCIs that can capture more of the expressivity and communication that is possible” than with current technologies, she adds.
“This gives us hope for neural prosthesis that will enter day-to-day usage,” says Christian Herff, a computational neuroscientist at Maastricht University in the Netherlands.
Multitasking challenges
The difficulty of decoding gestures and speech at the same time is that some of the neural signals that are involved overlap. And the patterns of neural activity can be slightly different during tasks that involve simultaneous speech and gesturing, compared with that during speech-only or gesture-only tasks.
To distinguish between the two, Brosler and her colleagues worked with two participants. The device — a surgically implanted array of 253 electrodes placed on the surface of the brain’s cortex — “covers a fairly large surface area of the sensorimotor cortex, so it can capture signals related to both speech and body movements”, explains Brosler.
The first participant had impaired speech and movement following a brainstem stroke. The researchers asked him to silently speak five phrases and attempt to wave, nod, shake his hands and clap.
The second participant had a type of motor neuron disease called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which caused progressive speech paralysis and motor impairments. At the time of the study, he was able to type messages on his computer and phone. The team asked him to vocalize ten phrases and imagine making ten gestures such as a shrug and thumbs up — without moving his body except for his facial muscles.
The BCIs recorded the participants’ neural activity when they attempted to speak or gesture, as well as when they used speech and gestures together, such as pairing the word ‘hello’ with a wave or pairing ‘yes’ with a head nod.

other-interests-9e0f3c8c6d.headline: Nearly forgotten languages are finding new words for Colombia’s dragonflies
other-interests-9e0f3c8c6d.fulltext:
Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.
When researchers began cataloging dragonflies in Guainía, a remote region in eastern Colombia, the scientific record contained only about 10 species. By working with Indigenous communities, they’ve found nearly 120.
“When we started, very little was known,” Yiselle Cano, biodiversity leader of the Dragones Guainía project, told contributor Manuel Fonseca for Mongabay.
“I think we must be close to 120 species by now,” Cano said. “It’s a hugely diverse group, because it includes dragonflies native to the Orinoco, Amazonas, and dragonflies that are endemic to the Guiana Shield.”
The diversity makes Guainía a hotspot for dragonflies and damselflies. It may also provide insights on what is happening to the region’s water. These insects depend on healthy freshwater ecosystems, and their aquatic habitats are coming under growing pressure from mining, deforestation, poorly managed waste, and rapidly expanding tourism.
Cataloging the insects was only part of the work. Once the researchers had begun filling gaps in the scientific record, they held workshops to share their findings with local communities. There they encountered another gap: the language of biology meant little to people whose understanding of the landscape had been formed outside scientific taxonomies. Some participants didn’t speak Spanish at all.
Community leaders invited everyone, from young children to elders who retained ancestral knowledge. As researchers displayed the dragonflies found around puddles, streams, and rivers, participants tried to identify them in their own languages.
“This is something that sometimes leaves us speechless,” Delio Suárez, a Tucano Indigenous leader of the multiethnic community La Ceiba, told Mongabay. “This leaves us with the task of recovering their names, of looking back and asking the last remaining wisdom keepers that we have.”
Sometimes the words could be recovered. Sometimes they had to be invented. In the community of Remanso, members of the Puinave tribe created names in an ancestral language that is itself at risk of disappearing. Tucano and Curripaco communities have also begun naming the insects while working to recover their languages.
Communities are now developing their own means of monitoring dragonflies and, through them, the condition of the water on which they depend.
Read the full story by Manuel Fonseca here.

beyond-your-beat-08a9d6c860.headline: ‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advert
beyond-your-beat-08a9d6c860.fulltext:
The US actor Sydney Sweeney is facing a backlash from female Olympians and other athletes, who have accused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sports by appearing in a controversial advert for a sports prediction company.
In the viral commercial for Novig, which was viewed more than 22 million times in the first two days of its release, Sweeney’s nude body is covered by footballs, basketballs, and other sports equipment, as she tells users they can bet on “just sports”. After saying “sports” nine times, she appears topless on a pool table, before saying: “You can’t trade this, I just look good here.”
The advert has led to a storm of protest led by the British sprinter Amy Hunt, who won four European Championship gold medals last month. After finishing fourth in the 200m at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday evening, Hunt said: “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening.”
That was a reference to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth-fastest women’s 200m, and Hunt went on to reveal the painful realities she and other sports stars faced. “When you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty,” she said. “It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time, definitely.
“There’s some low moments. Even turning up to this championship, my period started yesterday, so that’s not really ideal, and that’s not ever what you try to really plan for.”
The British Olympic cycling gold medallist Sophie Capewell was also deeply critical of the advert. “Imagine a world where sexualised representation isn’t the most popular way of seeing women in sport,” Capewell said on social media.
In Australia, there was also widespread fury with the four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus leading the charge. “I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” she wrote. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity.
“How do we live in a world where monetising a woman’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”
Hundreds of athletes took inspiration from the American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted footage of her competing under the message “this is what a woman in sport looks like” on an Instagram post that was liked more than a million times.
Sweeney appeared to respond to the criticism by posting a series of images of prominent female and male athletes posing naked for magazine shoots, including Serena Williams and the footballer Megan Rapinoe and the basketball player Sue Bird.
The public relationship consultant Mark Borkowski, who has worked with everyone from Mikhail Gorbachev to Diego Maradona, said he felt the advert was “cynical soft porn”, but that the controversy would benefit Novig “given the number of eyeballs on it”.
Borkowski said: “Sex still sells. And the outrage, the culture war argument gets you one thing: enormous reach.”
He also questioned whether Sweeney, who has starred in several successful TV series and films including Euphoria, The White Lotus and The Housemaid, may one day regret her decision.
“Sweeney will make a lot of money over a short span of time,” Borkowski said. “But often it is about how your brand sustains over the years, not in the first flourish. And this sort of promotion can come back to haunt people.”
The advert has been defended by Jacob Fortinsky, the founder and chief executive of Novig, which launched last month. “Sydney is great at captivating audiences and being the centre of attention,” he said. “In some sense, it forces us into the national discourse.”
Fortinsky also pushed back against criticisms of the adult nature of the content, pointing out that Novig is restricted to users aged 21 and older. He added that Sweeney had approached the company about an equity partnership and helped to craft its message.
This is not the first time an advert featuring Sweeney has attracted controversy. Last year American Eagle’s “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans” campaign used a play on “jeans” and “genes”, including references to the blue-eyed actor’s inherited traits, sparked a culture war, with some saying it invoked eugenics.
Several months after the controversy erupted, Sweeney said she had been unaware of it as she had been filming Euphoria. “Anyone who knows me knows that I’m always trying to bring people together,” she said. “I’m against hate and divisiveness.”
